definition: Narrative psychology is an approach to understanding selfhood and agency by focusing on the interpretive, story-like ways people make sense of their lived experiences and social position. In this packet, it is described as a context-sensitive perspective concerned with how people organize meaning under structurally unequal conditions.

reasons: The packet supports a context-sensitive, narrative-informed account of selfhood and agency under structural constraint, but it does not explicitly support the “story-like ways people make sense of their lived experiences” formulation.

The definition presents narrative psychology as a broader established approach rather than limiting the sense to the packet’s specific, preliminary framing of reflective selfhood and rural woman identity reinterpretation in one study.

The definition claims narrative psychology focuses on “interpretive, story-like ways people make sense” of experiences; the packet describes “interpretive processes” and “context-sensitive operationalizations,” but it does not explicitly support the “story-like” phrasing.

The remainder of the definition (context-sensitive perspective; interpretive meaning-making; selfhood and agency; structurally unequal conditions/structural constraint) is broadly consistent with the packet, but the unsupported “story-like” component is a substantive claim.
